title: What did a "sin-eater" do? | JOB ETYMOLOGY

entries.note: First a measure, how much a horse could carry, perhaps linked to [[from?:gob]]; Johnson called it low, petty work, and the occupation sense dates from the 1800s.
An older phrase that keeps the earlier sense of [[see:job]] as a measure, effectively a cartload of work.
Another name for a horse's load, alongside [[see:jobble]] and [[see:job]].
Another name for a horse's load, alongside [[see:jobbet]] and [[see:job]].
A lump of something, which the OED and other sources connect with [[see:job]]; today it suggests something gooey.
A Scottish word for a turd, which ties the idea of a [[see:job]] to something filthy.
From professing a vow on joining a guild, like a [[same-root:profession of faith]]; in the 17th century it became a euphemism for prostitution.
Given as a parallel for the vow-taking idea behind [[same-root:profession]].
A phrase that preserves the 17th-century use of [[see:profession]] as a euphemism for prostitution.
Once meant power, as it still does in other Germanic languages; English is the exception, where it now means skill, though [[see:witchcraft]] keeps the old sense.
Preserves the old sense of [[see:craft]] as power.
From a root meaning to grasp or seize; that suits military occupation, or more kindly, work that holds your attention.
In the 17th century it was considered rude because it was used as a euphemism for sex.
From the same Old English verb as [[same-root:tread]]: your trade is the path you choose to tread in life.
Comes from the same Old English verb as [[same-root:trade]].
Essentially to be folded into something; from the same source as [[same-root:implication]], meaning to enfold, involve or unite.
Shares its source with [[same-root:employ]].
[[see:William Shakespeare]] was the first to use it for a person who employs others; before that it meant someone who used an object. It made [[gave:employee]] possible.
The first to use [[see:employer]] for a person who employs another, as Rob found while making a video about him.
Could only exist once [[from:employer]] meant a person who employs others.
From the same Proto-Indo-European root as [[same-root:wright]], [[same-root:wrought]], [[same-root:energy]] and Greek [[same-root:ergon]].
Comes from the same root as [[same-root:work]].
Surprisingly, it comes from the same root as [[same-root:work]].
Means work and comes from the same root as [[same-root:work]]; the hosts covered it in their periodic table episode.
From Old English [[from:wyrhta]], worker; in Anglo-Saxon times nearly everyone seemed to be a wright or a [[see:smith]], and it survives as a surname.
The Old English [[see:wright]] word for a mason.
The Old English word for a carpenter and a favourite of both hosts; it was later replaced by [[see:carpenter]].
The Old English [[see:wright]] word for a potter.
An Old English word for a murderer; not a job as such, but something that defined you.
Found across the Germanic languages (German Schmied); from a Germanic root meaning skilled worker of any kind, not just in metal, hence the many kinds of smith.
One of Rob's favourites: an Icelandic [[see:smith]] word for a poet.
Started as a joke: [[see:Ben Jonson]], among its first users, mocked himself as a [[see:wordwright]] by comparing writing with manual trades like millwrights and wheelwrights.
A 17th-century playwright and one of the first to use [[see:playwright]], meant as a joke.
One of the manual wright trades that [[see:playwright]] poked fun at.
One of the manual wright trades that [[see:playwright]] poked fun at.
One of the manual wright trades that [[see:playwright]] poked fun at.
One of the manual wright trades that [[see:playwright]] poked fun at.
How [[see:Ben Jonson]] mockingly saw himself when he coined [[see:playwright]].
A slightly pretentious self-description, like [[see:wordwright]], that deliberately borrows the hands-on image of a [[see:smith]]; Rob calls Jess one.
A [[see:smith]] who worked with heavy metals.
A [[see:smith]] who worked with gold.
A [[see:smith]] who worked with silver.
A Latin-derived name for an ironworker, named after iron, who mostly made horseshoes because they were in such demand; also covered in the periodic table episode.
Replaced [[see:trēowwyrhta]]; from a Latin word for a cart or carriage, since the first carpenters made carts rather than any wooden object.
From French [[from:bouc]], goat: the first butchers sold only goat meat; the same word appears in [[same-root:buck]] and [[same-root:springbok]].
Contains the same goat word as [[same-root:butcher]].
Its 'bok', spelled with a K in Afrikaans and Dutch, is the same goat word as in [[same-root:butcher]].
Means bearder, but barbers also did surgery, pulled teeth and let blood, which explains the [[see:barber's pole]].
The red pole supposedly represents a bloody bandage, recalling the [[see:barber]]'s bloodletting.
An old-fashioned job title that Rob mentions in connection with the surgeon-barbers.
First a wholesaler who bought and sold in gross, from Latin [[from:grossarius]]; the trade was often in food.
Extended to food in the 16th century because food was often traded in gross; Americans use groceries far more than the British do.
Pretty much the only kind of [[see:grocer]] still named as such in England.
Buying in gross suggested simple, coarse components, which gave the 'ew' sense; the bulk idea gave its use as an intensifier. Compare German [[same-root:groß (German)]] and French [[same-root:gros]].
The German for big, one of the related words given alongside [[same-root:gross]].
The French for fat or wide, one of the related words given alongside [[same-root:gross]].
An old feminine agent ending, as in [[see:baxter]], [[see:webster]] and [[see:brewster]].
The female equivalent of a baker, an example of the [[see:-ster]] ending.
The female equivalent of a weaver, an example of the [[see:-ster]] ending.
The female equivalent of a brewer, an example of the [[see:-ster]] ending.
The usual agent-noun ending for words from Old English and other Germanic languages, as in [[see:baker]] and [[see:hunter]], though there are dozens of exceptions.
An agent ending that Latin-derived words sometimes take, as in [[see:governor]] and [[see:conductor]]; such words can sound more pretentious, like [[see:actor]].
A rarer agent ending, seen in [[see:bursar]], which went back to the Latin spelling.
A Germanic agent noun with the [[see:-er]] ending.
A Germanic agent noun with the [[see:-er]] ending.
A Latin-derived agent noun with the [[see:-or]] ending.
A Latin-derived agent noun with the [[see:-or]] ending.
A candle maker, from Latin [[from:candelarius]]; an exception to the agent-ending patterns.
A Germanic word first spelled sailer, later Latinized, perhaps to match [[see:tailor]].
Latin-derived but brought into line with the English [[see:-er]] pattern.
An ending on Latin-derived professions taken directly from French, as in [[see:sommelier]]; the -yer of [[see:lawyer]] and [[see:bowyer]] is a variant, from Latin -arius.
An example of the French [[see:-ier]] ending.
From a French word meaning pack: first an officer managing provisions, then a butler, then a wine steward running a wealthy family's wine stores.
Its -yer is a variant of the [[see:-ier]] ending, spelled however people heard it.
Its -yer is a variant of the [[see:-ier]] ending.
A college treasurer; an Anglo-Latin word first spelled with -er that reverted to the Latin spelling of [[from:bursa]], a bag or purse.
An example of how Latinate [[see:-or]] spellings can seem more pretentious.
A Latin-derived feminine ending that has fallen out of use, surviving in [[see:dominatrix]] and [[see:aviatrix]].
The first example of the [[see:-trix]] ending that came to mind.
A slightly whimsical example of the [[see:-trix]] ending.
A feminine job title that is falling out of use.
A feminine form still used, at least while the Oscars separate awards by gender.
A shoe mender of uncertain origin, perhaps French for to couple; recorded from the 14th century. Also a dessert named for its cobblestone-like topping.
The OED rejects linking [[see:cobbler]] to cobble together; cobble, meaning mend, is recorded only from the late 15th century and may be a back-formation from [[from?:cobbler]].
Recorded in the 14th century, for stones set together to form a street; Jess sees support in it for the cobble-together theory of [[see:cobbler]].
Means nonsense; it is rhyming slang from cobbler's awls, rhyming with [[see:balls]], meaning [[see:bollocks]].
The word that cobbler's awls rhymes with in [[see:cobblers]].
What [[see:cobblers]] ultimately means.
A Middle English word for a shoemaker, from French chaucier; not usually connected with [[see?:Geoffrey Chaucer]], though it might be.
A leather worker, named after [[from:cordovan]], a special leather from [[see:Córdoba]], Spain.
A special leather from [[see:Córdoba]], Spain, which gave [[gave:cordwainer]].
A word for a shoemaker, from [[from:Saint Crispin]], patron saint of shoemakers.
The patron saint of shoemakers, who gave [[gave:crispin]].
Meant a shoemaker or shoemaker's apprentice before it took its modern sense, as covered before.
The plain term, alongside the many older words like [[see:cobbler]], [[see:cordwainer]] and [[see:snob]].
Was once a job but now survives only as a surname.
First meant someone from [[from:Milan]], a fashionable textile centre whose merchants sold clothes and goods; it narrowed to a hat trader. It has nothing to do with mills.
A fashionable centre of textiles whose merchants gave [[gave:milliner]] its name.
The Spanish city that gave [[gave:cordovan]] leather and so [[see:cordwainer]].
A hat seller in American English, but in Britain a seller of sewing bits and bobs; first a seller of small wares, probably from [[from?:hapertas]].
Found in an old list of traded goods, its meaning is unknown, maybe a cloth or miscellaneous goods; it is assumed to have given [[gave?:haberdasher]].
Jess wonders whether [[see:hapertas]] meant something like this.
Meant to imitate the tink of the tools on the metal things tinkers repaired.
A barrel maker; the 'coop' part seems to be a Germanic word for a cask, tub or vat, related to [[same-root:chicken coop]].
Coop once meant both casks and large baskets before narrowing to a home for birds; related to [[same-root:cooper]].

From French [[from:tailleur]], a cutter; French specifies the cutter, as in [[see:tailleur de robes]], but English tailor only ever meant cloth-cutter. Shares its Latin source with [[same-root:tagliatelle]].
The French for a tailor who worked with cloth, specifying the kind of [[see:tailor]].
The French for a stonemason or even a sculptor, another kind of tailleur besides the [[see:tailor]].
The French for someone who cut bits of wood, another kind of tailleur besides the [[see:tailor]].
Cut pasta, from the same Latin word as [[same-root:tailor]]: tailored pasta.
A wigmaker, from [[from:peruke]], a wig, who made the big stylized wigs of past centuries.
A wig, especially a big elaborate one, also called a [[same-root:periwig]].
A big elaborate wig worn by men and many women; it sounds like an English take on French and gave [[gave:wig]].
A shortening of [[from:periwig]] from the 1670s, surprising both hosts, who had assumed wig came first; the fashion and word probably came from France.
To sell someone a [[see:wig]].
To lose your mind, from the earlier [[from:dash my wig]], from being so angry you throw your wig down.
An exclamation picturing someone so angry they throw their wig on the ground; it gave [[gave:wig out]].
A public fight or rumble, as if everyone threw their wigs down; compare [[equivalent:handbags at dawn]].
Rob's comparison for [[equivalent:wigs on the green]], with a similar idea.
Someone who polishes or maintains metal weapons or instruments; the name is a metathesis of [[from:furbish]].
The older form behind [[gave:frobisher]], from a French word for polishing, burnishing or mending; it survives in [[gave:refurbish]].
The modern word that keeps [[from:furbish]].
A worker who swapped full bobbins on a spinning frame for empty ones; also a carding-machine comb that strips off fibre; perhaps a do-offer, from [[from?:doff]].
As in doffing your cap, a contraction of do off; the hosts wonder whether [[gave?:doffer]] comes from it too.
A skilled woodworker who made chairs and furniture parts; bodging seems to be a variant of, or related to, [[same-root:botch]].
Meant to repair a worn or damaged item, specifically badly; related to [[same-root:bodger]].
Something just thrown together, not necessarily [[see:botch]]ed.
A Victorian who waded through London's sewers for items to salvage and sell; probably the source of [[gave?:tosh]].
Nonsense, thought to come from the junk the [[from?:tosher]] pulled out of the sewers.
An early street artist who made temporary chalk drawings on pavements; from [[from:screeve]].
Found in 'to screeve a fakement', writing a swindler's deceptive letter; a jarring variant related to [[same-root:scribe]] and French [[same-root:écrivain]].
Rob suggests it must be related to [[same-root:screeve]].
The French for writer, which Rob relates to [[same-root:screeve]].
Cleaned castle latrines from Norman times; gong is from Old English [[from:gang]], passageway, euphemistically a latrine.
The all-purpose version of the [[see:gong farmer]]'s job.
Hired to eat bread passed over a corpse, absorbing the dead person's sins; practised until the 17th or 18th century, and cited by Protestants against Catholic practice.
A horror-comedy novel built around [[see:sin-eater]]s that Jess recommends, the author's first adult novel.
Hired by local authorities or courts to test a district's beer strength; conner is from an Old English word meaning tester, unrelated to [[unrelated:con man]].
The con is short for confidence, as in confidence trickster or artist, because you win someone's confidence to swindle them; unrelated to [[unrelated:ale conner]].
An ethically dubious lawyer; petty means small and fogger a schemer, probably from Dutch for cheat, perhaps influenced by fogging the truth or by [[see?:pettifactor]].
A 16th-century public servant handling smaller cases; Jess wonders whether it turned into [[gave?:pettifogger]].
Someone called to the bar of justice; etymologically basically the same as [[same-root:barista]], a person who works at a bar.
Not found in English before the 1980s (an OED quote from 1982 about Rome); originally a bartender of coffee and alcohol alike, akin to [[same-root:barrister]].
Literally name caller: a Roman who reminded his office-seeking master of names, later someone announcing guests at galas; linked etymologically to [[same-root:nomenclature]].
Means name calling; linked to [[same-root:nomenclator]] only by etymology, not by usage.
A naval surgeon's assistant, perhaps also someone who served [[from?:loblolly]].
A thick porridge or gruel, the lob probably as in blob, suggesting lumpy or bubbling soup; also a ship's doctor.
A sailor's dish that gave [[gave:Scouser]].
The nickname for people from Liverpool, from [[from:lobscouse]].
An old contemptuous term for a doctor, from doctors' use of leeches.
An old contemptuous term for a doctor, alongside [[see:leecher]].
A doctor who tried to diagnose people by examining their urine.
An unpleasant nickname for a doctor that Rob prefers not to explain.
A fun-sounding but more or less nonsensical old name for a doctor.
An old name for a doctor that Rob thinks still fits a few today.
One of the old contemptuous names for a doctor.
One of the old contemptuous names for a doctor.
Latin for teacher; meant an adviser or religious teacher long before a medical practitioner, though it is still used loosely for anyone with a PhD.
Old English for both the doctor and the parasite; it's unclear which came first, or whether the animal was named after the doctors who used it.
An old healthcare worker, short for [[from:hospital]]; nothing to do with [[unrelated:spittle]].
Not always a place of healing; a place to stay, from a root meaning stranger, guest or host shared with [[same-root:hostile]], [[same-root:hospitality]], [[same-root:hostage]], [[same-root:hotel]].
From the same root as [[same-root:hospital]].
Given as an early sense of what a [[see:hospital]] could be.
From the same root as [[same-root:hospital]], one of the members of the family that turned pejorative.
From the same root as [[same-root:hospital]].
From the same root as [[same-root:hospital]].
Has nothing to do with [[unrelated:spittler]].
